title: Obfuscated Gradients Give a False Sense of Security: Circumventing Defenses to Adversarial Examples
authors: Anish Athalye, Nicholas Carlini, David Wagner

pages.title: A false sense of security
pages.subtitle: Why so many defenses only look robust

blocks.html: The point of this page: by 2018 the literature was full of published defenses against adversarial examples, several accepted at top venues. This paper makes an uncomfortable claim — most of them do not actually make models robust. They merely break the attacker's gradient, so gradient-based attacks fail and the defense only looks robust.

Shared vocabulary (used across this collection). An adversarial example is a tiny, usually imperceptible input change $\delta$ that flips the model's prediction; the threat model bounds $\delta$, here typically an $\ell_\infty$ ball of radius $\epsilon$ (every pixel may move by at most $\epsilon$). A white-box attacker sees the model and its gradients; a black-box attacker sees only outputs. Attacks like FGSM (one step) and PGD (many steps) all steer by the gradient of the loss with respect to the input.

The phenomenon: obfuscated gradients. The authors name a special case of gradient masking in which a defense produces gradients that are nonexistent, wrong, or unusable — so a gradient attack wanders uselessly — even though strong adversarial examples still exist. They identify three distinct ways this happens, give one practical circumvention per type, and apply them to the non-certified defenses at ICLR 2018.

The result. Of nine defenses examined, they fully circumvent seven and partially circumvent one, in most cases driving the defended model to near-zero accuracy under attack — within each defense's own claimed threat model.
We identify obfuscated gradients, a kind of gradient masking, as a phenomenon that leads to a false sense of security in defenses against adversarial examples.

Why it matters. The deeper contribution is a checklist of warning signs plus a small reusable toolkit of adaptive attacks (BPDA, EOT) that became required practice. After this paper, “we beat FGSM and PGD” stopped being acceptable evidence that a defense works.

pages.title: Gradient masking vs. real robustness
pages.subtitle: A broken gradient is not a strong model

blocks.html: The intuition. Every gradient-based attack needs one thing: a useful gradient $\nabla_x L$ pointing the way to higher loss. A defense can make that gradient useless two very different ways — (1) by being genuinely robust (the loss really is hard to raise inside the $\epsilon$-ball), or (2) by masking the gradient (the direction still exists, the attacker just can't read it). The second is a security illusion.

A concrete analogy. Imagine a safe. Real robustness is a thick steel door — no matter how the thief pushes, it won't open. Gradient masking is a door that is actually flimsy but coated in grease: the thief's hands slip, so casual attempts fail, yet a thief who wears gloves (an adaptive attack) opens it instantly. Testing only with bare hands tells you nothing about the door.
How to tell them apart. The authors give diagnostic signs that a defense is masking rather than robust. Each is something that should be impossible for a truly robust model:

items: One-step beats iterative: FGSM (one step) succeeds more than PGD (many steps). Impossible if the gradient were honest — more optimization should never do worse.
Black-box beats white-box: an attacker with no gradient access beats one with full access. Means the gradient is actively misleading.
Unbounded attacks fail: letting $\epsilon \to \infty$ (any change allowed) still doesn't reach 100% success. A real model must break when the attacker can replace the whole image.
Random sampling beats gradient descent: brute-force random search inside the ball finds adversarial examples that the gradient could not.
Non-monotone in $\epsilon$: increasing the budget does not smoothly increase attack success.

blocks.html: Why these work as a test. A genuinely robust model gets harder to attack as the attacker tries harder, and a large enough budget must eventually win (replace the panda with a gibbon outright). When the pattern inverts — effort hurts the attacker — the gradient is being masked, not the model hardened. Any one of these red flags is enough to be suspicious.

pages.title: Shattered, stochastic, and vanishing gradients
pages.subtitle: Three ways a gradient becomes useless

blocks.html: The question this page answers: how does a defense end up with a useless gradient? The authors find three distinct mechanisms, each with its own cause and its own cure. Naming them is what makes the cures systematic rather than one-off.

rows: Non-differentiable or discretizing preprocessing (JPEG, quantization, thermometer encoding), or a numerically wrong gradient
Gradient is nonexistent or incorrect — points nowhere useful
Randomized defenses (random crops/rotations, test-time dropout, random input transforms)
Gradient is correct for one random draw but noisy and inconsistent across draws
Very deep computation, e.g. unrolling many iterations of an optimization or a generative model before the classifier
Gradient blows up or decays to ~0 through the long chain

blocks.html: Concrete examples. Shattered: a defense that JPEG-compresses the input first — JPEG rounds to discrete blocks, so its derivative is zero almost everywhere, and PGD sees a flat surface. Stochastic: a defense that randomly crops the image at test time — the gradient depends on which crop you got, so it jitters. Vanishing: a defense that runs the input through 100 steps of a generative “purifier” before classifying — backpropagating through all 100 steps explodes or vanishes.

The unifying insight. In every case the adversarial example still exists; only the gradient signal is broken. So the fix is never “abandon gradient attacks” — it is “give the attacker back a usable gradient.” The next page gives exactly one tool per mechanism.

pages.title: BPDA and EOT: the circumvention tools
pages.subtitle: Approximate the missing gradient, average over randomness

blocks.html: Tool 1 for shattered gradients: Backward Pass Differentiable Approximation (BPDA). Suppose the defense applies a non-differentiable preprocessing $g$ before the network $f$, and on real inputs $g(x) \approx x$ (the transform roughly preserves the image — true of JPEG, quantization, denoisers). On the forward pass run the true $g$ so the attack is realistic; on the backward pass pretend $g$ is the identity so the gradient flows straight through it.

blocks.tex: \nabla_x \, f(g(x)) \;\approx\; \Big[ \nabla_z f(z) \Big]_{z = g(x)} \quad \text{using} \quad \frac{\partial g}{\partial x} \approx I \;\; (\text{since } g(x)\approx x)

blocks.html: Term by term: $f$ is the classifier, $g$ the preprocessing; $f(g(x))$ is the full defended model; $\nabla_z f(z)$ evaluated at $z=g(x)$ is the classifier's gradient at the preprocessed input; and $\partial g / \partial x \approx I$ (the identity) is the substitution — we replace the broken/zero Jacobian of $g$ with identity. The chain rule then leaves just the classifier's own (well-behaved) gradient. More generally you can swap in any smooth function that mimics $g$ on the backward pass.

Why it works. The defense was relying on $g$ to hide the gradient, but $g$ barely changes the image, so the true sensitivity of the output to the input is essentially the classifier's sensitivity. BPDA recovers exactly that and hands it to PGD, which then proceeds normally.

Tool 2 for stochastic gradients: Expectation Over Transformation (EOT). If the defense applies a random transform $t$ drawn from a distribution $T$, don't attack one random draw — attack the model in expectation by averaging the gradient over many sampled transforms.

Term by term: $t \sim T$ samples a random transform (e.g. a random crop/rotation); $f(t(x))$ is the defended output for that draw; $\mathbb{E}_{t\sim T}[\cdot]$ is the average over all draws. The equality (gradient of the average = average of the gradients) lets us estimate it by sampling $n$ transforms $t_1,\dots,t_n$ and averaging their gradients. This cancels the noise and yields a stable direction that raises the loss on average over the randomness.

Tool 3 for exploding/vanishing gradients. When the defense unrolls a long iterative computation, don't backpropagate through every step. Reparameterize the optimization or apply BPDA over the iterative component — treat the whole purification loop as an approximate identity on the backward pass — so the gradient never has to traverse the unstable chain. Often this combines with BPDA/EOT for defenses that mix several tricks.

The pattern. Three mechanisms, three recovery techniques, all built on the same principle: the adversarial direction is still there; restore an honest estimate of it and standard PGD finishes the job.

The experiment. The authors take the non-certified defenses accepted at ICLR 2018, diagnose which obfuscation type each relies on, and apply the matching tool. Of nine defenses, seven turn out to rely on obfuscated gradients and are fully circumvented; one more is partially circumvented. In most cases defended accuracy under the adaptive attack drops to 0% or near 0% — inside each defense's own claimed $\epsilon$ budget.

rows: Input transform / quantization (e.g. input transformations, thermometer encoding, pixel deflection)
Randomized input (e.g. random resizing/padding, stochastic activation pruning)

blocks.html: The consistent pattern. Input transforms and quantization fall to BPDA; randomized defenses fall to EOT; long generative/iterative pipelines fall to a combination. In no case did the masking translate into actual robustness once the attacker was handed back a usable gradient. The defenses were grease on a flimsy door.

The telling exception. The one category that survived was PGD adversarial training (Madry et al., also in this collection) — the defense that does not hide gradients but genuinely solves the saddle-point problem. That contrast is the paper's central piece of evidence: real robustness and gradient masking are fundamentally different things, and only the former survives an attacker who knows the defense.

pages.title: How to evaluate a defense honestly
pages.subtitle: Adaptive attacks as a requirement, not an option

blocks.html: The methodology shift. This paper reset the standards of the whole subfield. After it, evaluating a defense only against fixed, off-the-shelf attacks became unacceptable. A defense must be tested against an adaptive attack — one designed with full knowledge of exactly how the defense works — and the diagnostic warning signs must all come out the right way.

items: Always run a strong iterative attack (PGD) with many steps and random restarts — not just FGSM.
If preprocessing is non-differentiable, attack it with BPDA; do not conclude robustness from a dead gradient.
If the defense is randomized, attack it with EOT, averaging the gradient over the randomness.
Check the warning signs: iterative should beat one-step, white-box should beat black-box, and unbounded $\epsilon$ should reach 100% success.
Be suspicious of any defense whose robustness vanishes the moment you give the attacker a better gradient.

blocks.html: We believe that future defenses should be evaluated against adaptive attacks designed with full knowledge of the defense.

How it connects. The core trick — “attack the real quantity, not the masked gradient you're shown” — is the same insight C&W used to break defensive distillation (attack the logits, not the saturated softmax). This paper generalizes it into a reusable toolkit and a checklist. Together with FGSM (mechanism), C&W (strong attack), and PGD/Madry (the defense that actually holds), it is the “how we measure progress” pillar of adversarial robustness.

A common misconception it corrected. A high robust-accuracy number is not evidence of robustness unless the attack was strong and adaptive. Many of the broken defenses reported excellent numbers — against weak attacks. The number means nothing without the threat model and the adaptive attack behind it.
